opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not that much, and I think anyone in AI should be pretty humble about that. If you'd asked people two years before ChatGPT what the world would look like, almost nobody would have gotten it right, including people inside the labs. The field moves in a way where the important thing often isn't on anyone's roadmap.

That said, I'd separate two kinds of predictions. Some things I'm fairly confident about, because they're driven by trends that are already in motion. Models will keep getting more capable, especially on reasoning and on longer-horizon tasks. Agents will move from demos into actually doing real work in more places, like coding, research assistance, and operations. And the cost of a given level of intelligence will keep dropping. Those are almost extrapolations.

What I'm much less confident about is the shape of things: which products win, how people actually end up using these systems, what the interface looks like, how the economics settle, how society reacts. That's where the surprises come from. Technology is maybe the easier part to predict. How it gets absorbed into the world is much harder.

One thing I've come to believe is that we've spent a lot of effort on the first half of AI, which is building better methods and climbing benchmarks. The second half is more about defining the right problems and evaluating real-world utility. If that shift happens, a lot of what matters in two years will depend on questions people haven't framed well yet. So I'd say I have reasonable confidence in the direction and very low confidence in the details. I try to hold my views loosely and update quickly.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes confidence in broad trends from confidence in details, but it does not distinguish imagining a possible future from reliably predicting what the world will actually be like.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not much. I think one of the things I've learned from working in this field is that the people who sound most confident about two years out are usually the ones who end up being most wrong, and I include my past self in that.

If you'd asked me in 2022, before ChatGPT, what things would look like in 2024, I don't think I would have predicted that agents would become the central narrative of the whole industry so quickly. I was working on ReAct at the time, and even then I thought of it as kind of a niche research direction. The idea that every major lab would reorganize around "agents" within a couple of years, that wasn't obvious to me.

So I'd say my confidence in specific predictions is low. But I do think there's a difference between predicting specific outcomes and predicting the shape of things. The shape I'm fairly confident about: models will keep getting better at doing longer, more autonomous tasks. The bottleneck is shifting from "can the model reason" to "can we define the task well, evaluate it well, and give it the right environment." That trend I'm pretty confident in, because it's not really a prediction about technology, it's more a prediction about where the hard problems are.

Where I'm genuinely uncertain is on things like what the economic impact looks like, which products actually win, how fast adoption happens in the real world versus in demos. Those depend on people and institutions, not just on models, and that's much harder to forecast.

I guess the honest answer is that I try to hold my predictions loosely and update fast. Being right about the direction and wrong about the timeline is a pretty common failure mode in AI, and I'd rather be humble about the timeline than pretend I know.

r001.rationale: The response says confidence in specific predictions is low and separates predicting specific outcomes from forecasting broad trends. It does not distinguish imagining a possible future from reliably predicting what will actually happen.

astra-6.text:
Not very much, especially when it comes to AI. Two years is long enough for a technical breakthrough to change the direction of things, but short enough that practical constraints can keep an apparently obvious change from happening. So even if you get the direction right, you can be very wrong about the timing.

I find predictions more useful as a way to expose assumptions than as statements about what will happen. What would need to be true for this future to arrive? What evidence would make me change my mind? I’d rather have a few possible scenarios and keep updating them than be very confident in one picture of the world two years from now.

r001.rationale: The response treats future scenarios as possibilities to explore and update, while expressing low confidence that they reliably predict what the world will actually be like.

sol-6.1.text:
Honestly, not very much—at least when it comes to detailed predictions. Two years is a long time in AI. You can have a reasonable view about the direction of progress, but the timing, the bottlenecks, and how people actually use the technology are much harder to predict.

I find it more useful to ask: what would have to be true for a particular future to happen? Then you can watch those assumptions and update your view. I’d put more confidence in that process than in a vivid picture of what the world will look like two years from now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts having a view of possible future directions or a vivid picture with reliably predicting what will happen, noting that detailed outcomes and their timing are hard to predict.
